chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Isma'il ibn Yasar al-Hashimi from Ali ibn Abdillah ibn Ghaleb al-Qaysi from al-Hasan al-Sayqal, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who said: 'The first slave I acquire will be free,' and he acquired six. He (peace be upon him) said: 'His intention was only for one, so let him choose whichever he wishes and emancipate him.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These narrations do not contradict what we previously stated, that emancipation is not valid before ownership, because the explanation in these narrations is that the man made that a vow to Allah the Exalted. If so, he is obliged to fulfill it. If it were not a vow, his preceding statement would have no effect, nor would fulfillment be obligatory upon him. It is permissible that the meaning is if the man wishes to fulfill what he said, even if it were not a vow. How is the ruling in that case? As for what the first two narrations included regarding the use of the lot, it is acted upon and is also the more cautious approach. And if a person acted according to the last narration and chose one of them and emancipated him, he would not be mistaken.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man says 'the first slave I buy is free' but buys more than one?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the ruling for a man who vows to free the first slave he acquires but obtains multiple, establishing that his specific intention (*niyyah*) limits the obligation to one. Shaykh al-Tusi’s commentary contextualizes this as a vow (*nadhr*) to God, where fulfillment is obligatory, and notes that while drawing lots is the safer (*ahwat*) method, direct selection is also legally valid. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of balancing textual literalism with the underlying intent of the vow-giver.
